name: Mesogun

lead: A mesogun is a handheld device that fires many tiny injections into the skin quickly. It is used in mesotherapy to deliver substances such as hyaluronic acid, vitamins or PRP, mostly to the face.
Research specific to the device is limited to a lab delivery study, a hydration study and a few case reports.

paras: A spring or pressure mechanism pushes small amounts of solution into the dermis at each press, avoiding repeated manual injections. A lab study on ink in foam and pig skin examined how the fluid is delivered.

Reported problems include a rosacea flare after an injection through a stamp-type microneedle and infection clusters after mesotherapy in Australia. Regulation of what gets injected varies by country.

lead: A mesogun is a handheld, spring- or pressure-driven injector used in mesotherapy to deliver many small intradermal injections of a solution in quick succession, typically across the face. [1][2] The solutions used in aesthetic practice include hyaluronic acid, vitamins, and, in some clinics, platelet-rich plasma. [3][4]

Mesotherapy itself is described by Wikipedia as an alternative-medicine technique that injects drugs, enzymes, vitamins, plant extracts or hyaluronic acid just below the skin, and notes that cosmetic uses have not been tested in standard clinical trials. [5] Published work specifically on mesogun devices is small: a laboratory study of delivery behaviour, a trial of a stamp-type microneedle injector for skin hydration, and case reports including an adverse reaction. [1][3][6]
infobox: Mesotherapy: intradermal delivery of hyaluronic acid, vitamins, PRP
Varies by country; solutions injected are chosen by practitioner

paras: Mesoguns allow a practitioner to deliver numerous shallow injections without manually repeating each one. A 2017 report in the Journal of Cutaneous and Aesthetic Surgery described a spring-loaded syringe for multiple rapid injections, a related design concept. [2] A stamp-type variant carries a small cluster of microneedles that is pressed against the skin and injects the solution at each press. [3][6]

A 2016 study in Skin Research and Technology tested a commercial mesogun, a locally made intradermal injector and manual syringe injection by injecting blue ink into polyurethane foam and pig skin, in order to examine how the fluid is delivered. The authors framed the work as the first evaluation of the mechanism of transdermal delivery in mesotherapy. [1]

A 2020 study in Dermatologic Therapy investigated a stamp-type microneedle injector (sold as Dermashine balance and described in the title as a mesogun injector) delivering hyaluronic acid into the dermis, with the stated aim of maintaining skin hydration; the study assessed efficacy and safety for skin hydration. [3]

A 2021 report described seven patients with corticosteroid-induced rosacea-like dermatitis given two sessions of platelet-rich plasma mesotherapy before routine treatment. [4] A 2026 case series used high-frequency ultrasound to assess PRP injection for facial photoaging. [7] These studies concern the injected substance more than the device.
A 2022 case report described rosacea aggravated after intracutaneous injection of poly-L-lactic acid through a stamp-type microneedle. [6]

Wikipedia's mesotherapy article reports clusters of skin abscesses and a mycobacterial infection in Australia after treatment, and notes that the US FDA does not control what practitioners inject, which is overseen by state medical boards. Several South American countries ban mesotherapy, and France briefly banned it for fat removal in 2011 before the ban was lifted. [5]
